content: Scabies is a highly pruritic skin condition caused by the Sarcoptes scabiei mite, and it represents a significant global public health issue, with an estimated 300 million cases worldwide. Some medications used to treat scabies have been associated with serious adverse effects, necessitating a thorough evaluation of their safety and efficacy. A systematic review was conducted to assess the effectiveness of both topical and systemic treatments for scabies. The search for relevant studies was performed in June 2010 using multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, and INDMED. Additional searches of grey literature and trial registries were conducted in August 2010. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating drug treatments for scabies were included in the analysis. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the trials and extracted data, with results presented as risk ratios (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The review included 22 small trials involving a total of 2,676 participants. Among these, one trial was placebo-controlled, 18 trials compared two or more drug treatments, three trials compared different treatment regimens, and one trial compared different drug vehicles. In a small placebo-controlled trial with 55 participants, oral ivermectin demonstrated fewer treatment failures by day seven compared to placebo. Topical permethrin was found to be more effective than oral ivermectin in two trials involving 140 participants. Additionally, permethrin was superior to topical crotamiton (194 participants, 2 trials) and topical lindane (753 participants, 5 trials) in terms of treatment efficacy. Permethrin also showed greater effectiveness in reducing persistent itching compared to crotamiton (94 participants, 1 trial) and lindane (490 participants, 2 trials). No significant differences in treatment failure rates were observed between permethrin and a natural pyrethrin-based topical treatment (40 participants, 1 trial) or between permethrin and benzyl benzoate (53 participants, 1 trial), although these trials were small. Similarly, no significant differences were detected between crotamiton and lindane (100 participants, 1 trial), lindane and sulfur (68 participants, 1 trial), benzyl benzoate and sulfur (158 participants, 1 trial), or benzyl benzoate and natural synergized pyrethrins (240 participants, 1 trial). All of these were topical treatments. Notably, no trials evaluating malathion were identified. No serious adverse events were reported in the included trials. However, some participants receiving topical treatments experienced skin reactions. Occasional reports of systemic side effects, such as headache, abdominal pain, diarrhea, vomiting, and hypotension, were also noted. In conclusion, topical permethrin appears to be the most effective treatment for scabies, while oral ivermectin is also an effective option. Further research is needed to evaluate the efficacy of malathion, particularly in comparison to permethrin, and to explore strategies for managing scabies in institutional and community settings.
